title: Mechanistic registry to study whether infection with Corona Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) accelerates atherosclerotic plaque progression
text:
The COVID-CT Registry is a study to determine if coronary artery disease patients with a history of COVID-19
infection in New York City have more inflammation, resulting in faster development of plaque in their coronary
arteries. CAT scans of the heart’s arteries will be used to measure inflammation, stenosis (narrowing of the
blood vessels), and plaque (cholesterol deposits) which are all associated with major cardiac events.

title: Investigating the mechanisms of Arc-dependent synaptic plasticity
text:
We recently discovered a new type of intercellular communication pathway: Arc, a gene critical for memory and
long-lasting forms of synaptic plasticity, forms virus-like capsids that transport proteins and RNA cell-to-cell. The
goal of this proposal is to investigate the mechanisms of Arc intercellular signaling and synaptic plasticity. Arc
dysregulation is implicated in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders; thus, our work will help determine
mechanisms of cognition and memory.

title: Tissue engineered organ-specific cancer metastasis model for cancer research
text:
Our application aims to apply advances in tissue engineering to address the need for the
development of cancer metastasis model that can reflect in vivo biology. We aim to engineer a
novel cancer metastasis model that can reflect organ-specificity and validate this model using
kidney cancer. Success of this application will provide a powerful new tool for cancer research
and reveal new cancer biology.

title: Development and validation of an LC-MS/MS method for identification and quantitation of emerging Fusarium and Alternaria mycotoxins in livestock and pet feed
text:
Successful completion of this project will allow for accurate, precise quantitation of emerging Fusarium
and Alternaria mycotoxins in pet food and livestock feed. These emerging mycotoxins pose a significant
risk to the health of companion animals and livestock animals, as well as to human health through
consumption of food derived from livestock. Having a robust, well-validated method for their
surveillance and for investigative work will increase our knowledge of these mycotoxins, help to close
the gaps in their safety and risk assessments, and prevent exposures to high levels of these toxins.

title: Development of biological structural tools for the study of protein-DNA complexes
text:
The goal of this project is to develop new, robust, and versatile mass spectrometry-
based tools capable of characterizing complex biomolecular systems and provide
structural information, not accessible using traditional tools. The new technologies will be
applied to model systems associated with several fundamental biological processes,
including gene regulation, DNA repair, replication, transcription, translation, and
recombination. In particular, the MS-based technologies proposed can study intrinsically
disordered and dynamic biomolecular systems and will significantly advance our
understanding of the biological machinery associated with disease mechanisms,
identification of therapeutic targets and disease prevention.

title: Decoding the Mechanisms for Selective Retinotectal Circuit Wiring
text:
The mammalian central nervous system is made up of many different types of neurons that form specific
connections, enabling complex neural processes such as the detection and processing of visual features. We
aim to use the connections between the mouse retina and superior colliculus as a model to study the role of
the cadherin family of cell recognition molecules in the wiring of the retinotectal circuit. Our overall objective is
to gain insight into the principles governing cadherin-mediated connectivity in the early visual pathway, to
understand how neurons are organized in the central nervous system, and, ultimately, to develop new
treatments for diseases affecting the eye and the brain.

title: Protective immunity to HCV and rational vaccine design
text: Scientific Core: Viral Immunity Core. Summary The Viral Immunity Core will be utilized to provide unique viral reagents and specialized services within this program related to the rodent HCV-like hepacivirus model. For instance, the Viral Immunity Core will be used to supply heterologous viral stocks and map viral sequencing mutations potentially arising after infectious challenge in determining if the rationally designed vaccine modalities and their enhanced immunogenicity translate to increased breadth of protection against heterologous viral variants. The most significant and unique strength of the Viral Immunity Core of HCV U19 program is access to animal HCV-like viruses, their genomic clones, and expertise in developing both rat and mouse models of infection. We isolated RHV-rn1 from a wild rat, developed its genome clone, and shared it with others; RHV-rn1 causes chronic infection in 90-100% of lab rats. Thus, the RHV-rn1 rat model is relevant for testing vaccines to prevent chronic HCV-like infection. Recently, we isolated a divergent RHV variant, Rn-2, which, after more than 25 passages in immunocompetent mice, acquired the ability to evade immunity and establish chronic infection in 129S1 and CC040 mice. The Viral Immunity Core has access to rat MHC class I and class II tetramers for multiple RHV proteins. The rat MHC class I tetramers were the first produced by the NIH Core for rats after we provided the rat MHC class I clone, indicating that we are capable of mapping T cell epitopes, MHC restriction, validation, and their use for analysis for immunogenicity of vaccines, nature of T cells, isolation for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and tracking their frequencies and functions in vaccinated animals. We propose the following specific aims for the Viral Immunity Core. Specific Aim 1 is to develop diverse RHV stocks, immune escape mutants, and random mutants for homologous and heterologous challenge in vaccinated rats. Specific Aim 2 is to support research projects in virus genome sequencing related to potential immune pressure-induced escape mutations, scRNA-seq, and bioinformatics. the Viral Immunity Core significantly enhances the overall significance of the project by utilizing the RHV and rodent models for the preclinical evaluation of HCV vaccine designs developed through the Research projects, and by ensuring the availability of well-characterized reagents, rigorous analytics, and data reproducibility across the program.

title: Cocaine Self-Administration and Drd2 Splicing Variants
text:
Cocaine use disorder is a chronic disease with continued devastating public health consequences, yet there
are currently no FDA-approved pharmacotherapies, highlighting an urgent need to identify new therapeutic
targets and underlying mechanisms. This project will investigate a novel mechanism by which cocaine-seeking
and taking behavior is modulated by cocaine-sensitive transcript variants of the dopamine D2 receptor gene in
preclinical models. Findings from this project will advance understanding of how genetic variations in the
dopamine D2 receptor gene contribute to cocaine use disorder and may inform development of targeted
therapies.

title: Somatic mutation rates in healthy aging
text:
Genetic mutations accumulate in every cell of our bodies throughout our lives, and these mutations have long
been thought to be an important reason why our bodies age. However, it is not known whether some people
accumulate mutations at a faster or slower rate with age, and whether differences in the rate at which
mutations occur might predict how long we live and the risk for aging-related diseases. This study will answer
these questions by measuring the mutation rate of a large number of people, which may allow us to predict,
and understand why, people age differently.

title: Improving the patient experience of hemodialysis vascular access decision making
text:
Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), who use hemodialysis as their kidney replacement method,
require vascular access in the form of an arteriovenous fistula, arteriovenous graft, or central venous catheter
to receive life-sustaining hemodialysis. Increasing evidence indicates that outcomes of the different vascular
access types vary widely based on patient characteristics, so much so that the recent update of the National
Kidney Foundation Dialysis Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guidelines states “…there is insufficient
evidence for KDOQI to make recommendations on choice of incident vascular access type,” leaving providers
and patients to select a vascular access type without adequate evidence of likely outcomes. To overcome this
key barrier, the goal of this R01 proposal is to optimize the patient experience of vascular access decision-
making by a) developing an interactive, evidence-based guide to vascular access outcomes that incorporates a
prognostic model for short and long-term outcomes of vascular access and b) identifying best practices for
utilization of the guide during the clinician-patient encounter.

title: Chemical membrane labeling and fluorescence-guided sequencing to decode microvesicle-mediated cell-cell communication
text:
Cellular exchange of microvesicles has been demonstrated to contribute to tumor progression, immune
evasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. This proposal aims to develop enabling technology for the
molecular analysis of microvesicle-mediated cell-cell communication. The enhanced understanding of
microvesicle-associated signaling, cell adaptation, and novel underpinnings of tumor progression will lead to
improved cancer diagnostics and therapeutics.

title: Multiomic single cell and spatial interrogation of mechanisms in cellular adaptation to stress
text:
Cellular response and adaptation to stress is a fundamental aspect of normal tissue homeostasis, and in cancer,
cellular adaptation manifests detrimentally as cancer cell resistance to therapy. This project addresses the
current lack of methods for multiome single-cell and spatial fate tracking and computational cell fate prediction
in systems where cell population dynamics are shaped by survival and adaptation. The proposed experimental
and computational methods are generally applicable to the study of time-dependent cellular processes in biology
and medicine, and the data generated will advance our understanding of drug resistance in cancer.

title: Importance of small GTPases in photoreceptor function
text:
This project will identify the importance of tubulin modifications and the small GTPase ARL13B in the health of
light-sensing photoreceptor cells. With a thorough understanding of the basic biology behind photoreceptor
health, we hope to identify novel therapies for patients with inherited blindness.

title: A Testing Program to Identify Novel Agents for Treatment of Pediatric and AYA High-Risk Sarcoma, Kidney and Liver Cancer
text:
Studies to be undertaken will continue to identify novel new agents and drug combinations that are active in
preclinical models of pediatric solid tumors. This group will focus on models of high-risk sarcoma, liver, and
kidney cancers that have been molecularly characterized.

title: ARCHS4: Massive Mining of Publicly Available RNA Sequencing Data
text:
The project will develop algorithms and software that will enhance the reuse of publicly available RNA-seq data.
The resource will enable cancer researchers to form more informed hypotheses about tumor molecular evolution;
and this work will lead to the identification of key molecular drivers as potential novel targets for the treatment of
various complex human cancers.

title: Inflammatory crosstalk between macrophages and stromal cells in clonal hematopoiesis
text: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) arises from somatic mutations such as in JAK2 or TET2 that provide a fitness advantage to hematopoietic stem cells and outgrowth of clones of blood cells. CH, which increases in frequency with aging, has emerged as a major independent risk factor for CVD. Studies in Tet2-/- and Jak2VF mouse models indicate a central role of macrophage inflammasome activation. In collaboration with Drs Tabas and Reilly, we have shown increased atherosclerosis, defective efferocytosis, increased necrosis and inflammatory myeloid cell populations in mice expressing Jak2VF in hematopoietic cells. Inhibition of the inflammasome product lL-1β improved features of plaques stabilization including increased fibrous caps and decreased necrotic cores. The overall hypothesis is that in several forms of CH including Jak2VF and Tet2, inflammasome activation and IL-1 release from mutant cells promote adverse changes in WT Μφs and stromal cells to induce plaque destabilization. These studies will synergize with those proposed by Drs Tabas and Zhang that are probing the mechanisms of defective efferocytosis and thinning of lesional fibrous caps which are key features of atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability and the major PPG theme. In Aim 1 we will assess the impact of Jak2VF-CH on bystander cells in lesions focusing on CH Μφ - WT Μφ crosstalk. We will use scRNAseq to evaluate the hypothesis that IL-1 secretion from Jak2VF Μφs reduces efferocytic Trem2Hi Μφs and increases inflammatory Μφs. We will employ novel Trem2 stabilizing antibodies to block Trem2 cleavage by IL-1, introduce a transgenic non-cleavable form of MerTK developed by Dr Tabas and in collaboration with Dr Zhang introduce deficiency of Pdcd6ip a novel negative regulator of efferocytosis, to see if these potential therapeutic approaches improve efferocytosis, necrotic core and fibrous cap formation. In Aim 2 we will assess the impact of Jak2VF- and Tet2-/-- CH on Μφ-fibroblast crosstalk. scRNAseq and SMC fate mapping with Dr Reilly shows that IL-1β inhibition in Jak2VF and Tet2 CH mice increases non-SMC-derived fibroblasts in fibrous caps. We will use fate mapping studies to assess the hypothesis that fibroblasts are derived from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). Aim 3 will involve translational studies in human carotid plaques. We will collaborate with Dr Maegdefessel, Tabas, Zhang and the Munich Vascular Biobank to test the hypothesis that CH mutations in TET2, JAK2 and DNMT3A are associated with increased inflammatory Μφs and decreased Trem2Hi Μφs in carotid plaques with adverse impact on features of plaque stability. Cells expressing inflammatory or pro-resolving genes will be visualized at single cell resolution in advanced vs early plaques and in unstable vs stable plaques. These collaborative studies may reveal novel genes and pathways acting downstream of inflammasome activation in clonal hematopoiesis to destabilize plaques and point to new and more precisely targeted therapeutic approaches that are less immunosuppressive than global inhibition of IL-1β or inflammasomes.

title: Identification of gene regulatory networks controlling temporal patterning in retinal progenitor cells and neurogenic Müller glia
text:
During retinal development, progenitor cells show dramatic changes in their ability to proliferate and
generate specific cell types, a process which is known as temporal patterning. We have recently identified
many genes that are dynamically expressed in progenitors during retinal development. We plan to test whether
and how they regulate temporal patterning during development and determine whether they can induce mature
retinal glial cells to reprogram into progenitor cells that generate early-born neuronal cell types such as retinal
ganglion cells and cone photoreceptor receptors. These studies have the potential to form the basis for
effective for cell-based therapies aimed at restoring vision in degenerative blinding diseases such as macular
degeneration and glaucoma.

title: GABA and NPY Signaling Interact to Shape Inhibition in the Auditory Tectothalamic Pathway
text:
Inhibitory circuits in the auditory tectothalamic pathway critically shape speech and vocalization processing,
sound localization and other neural computations that are crucial for hearing. This proposal aims to determine
how GABA and NPY signaling, from a distinct class of inferior colliculus (IC) neurons, work in concert to shape
sound processing in the IC and auditory thalamus. Furthermore, this proposal will determine how NPY signaling
can enhance detection of auditory cues in a mouse model of aging. The results of this proposal will provide
important new information about how a defined inhibitory neural circuit contributes to the ability of IC and thalamic
neurons to produce selective responses to communication sounds. In addition, this research will provide a
mechanistic foundation for the development of therapeutic agents to manipulate inhibitory signaling to improve
hearing for those who suffer from age-related hearing loss.

title: Mechanisms Underlying Tfh Cell Dysfunction in Early-Life Obesity
text:
Obesity during pregnancy and early childhood is a growing global health concern and is associated with impaired
vaccine responses and increased susceptibility to infections in children. This project will define how maternal
and early-life obesity reprograms CD4+ T cells to impair the differentiation and function of T follicular helper (Tfh)
cells—key regulators of humoral immunity—by reducing expression of the ubiquitin-modifying enzyme A20.
These studies will uncover foundational mechanisms of immune dysfunction in early-life obesity and identify
potential therapeutic targets to enhance vaccine efficacy and protective immune responses against infections in
vulnerable pediatric populations.

title: The Blockade of Siglec-15 as a Novel Approach to Improve Skeletal Integrity and Fracture Healing in Chronic SCI
text:
Approximately 42,000 Veterans are living with chronic spinal cord injury (SCI) in the United States. SCI often
leads to an extremely sedentary lifestyle and marked bone loss that is associated with an increased life-long risk
of fractures, morbidity, and financial burden. To date, there is no practical approach to safely and efficaciously
treat osteoporosis and bone fractures in Veterans with chronic SCI. This study will test if a novel agent, an
antibody against a bone cell receptor (Siglec-15) with unique bone-preserving and bone-building activity, can
safely improve skeletal integrity, strength, and fracture healing in a preclinical model of chronic SCI and severe
bone loss below the level of lesion. The proposed study will clarify basic mechanisms of novel processes that
control bone cell function, thereby improving efforts to reverse SCI-related deterioration of bone. If successful,
the proposed treatment can be swiftly deployed in a clinical trial and, ultimately, to clinical care with greater
promise to improve skeletal health in Veterans with chronic SCI than that of currently available treatment options.
